916.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse at (“at, by, to; infinitive marker”), from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, toward”). The use as an infinitive marker developed from the directional meaning of the preposition, comparable to the use of English to, German zu and French à before infinitives.
The word was officially written ⟨at⟩ in Norwegian until the spelling reform of 1917. In ordinary speech it was already generally pronounced /ɔ/, while /at/ survived as a formal reading pronunciation; the new spelling ⟨å⟩ reflected the common spoken form.
Compare Danish at, Swedish att, Icelandic að and Faroese at (“infinitiv / Inherited from Old Norse hvar (“where; how”). A dialectal reflex of the Old Norse interrogative adverb. Standard Bokmål hvor (“where; how”) instead continues the corresponding Danish form hvor, from Old Danish hwar.
The inherited adverb retained both its locative meaning “where” and its use as a degree adverb meaning “how; to what extent”.
Compare Swedish var, Icelandic hvar and Faroese hvar (“where”).

1000340.etyen:
Borrowed from French jujube (“jujube”), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *zizūpus (“jujube”), probably transmitted through Old Occitan or Occitan, although no corresponding Occitan form of the jujube type is attested. Compare Latin zīzyphus (“jujube tree”) for the tree sense and zīzyphum (“jujube fruit”), alongside zizufum, zizuphum and zizuphon, for the fruit sense. The Latin forms are borrowed from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon, “jujube tree”), of uncertain origin.

1004948.etyen: boble (“bubble”) + anorakk (“anorak”), literally “bubble anorak”, referring to an anorak made of boblestoff (“padded fabric”). The first element, boble (“bubble”), is derived from the verb boble (“to bubble”), ultimately from Middle Low German bubbeln (“to bubble”), an onomatopoeic formation. The second element, anorakk, ultimately reflects Greenlandic annoraaq (“anorak, fur overall”), from Proto-Inuit *atnuʀaaq (“clothing”), ultimately connected with Proto-Eskimo *atə- (“to put on”), although the precise formation of the Proto-Inuit word is uncertain.
